narrative:
The model determined that you have a 73% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school, compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students, signaled to the model that you would likely struggle on the bar. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. At 3.20 it sits very close to the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it helped your case modestly but could not overcome the effect of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 31 was also below the 37 average of accepted applicants, and your lower-middle family income is relatively uncommon among those who are admitted. However, these played smaller roles than your academic standing in law school.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving these areas would significantly improve your chances in a future application. (218 words)
